Apple  ➡️  https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast...


Emil is an incredibly strong boulderer with a particular talent for compression and sloper problems, along with harnessing dynamic movement. He has sent loads of the world’s toughest blocks, flashing up to V12 and redpointing up to V15, which he accomplished on the Dave Graham test piece, Story of Two Worlds. He documented that process beautifully on his YouTube Channel – which has over 100k subscribers and is growing fast. He has a real talent for bringing us viewers into his process, riding the rollercoaster of emotions from beginning to end. He also creates fantastic training content, most famous of which is probably the No Hang Protocol video he put out a couple years ago and went viral. Emil really exemplifies the intangible traits that make elite climbers who they are – an incredible work ethic, unstoppable passion, and seemingly unlimited psych to dig deeper and try harder than even seems possible.

However it can be hard to really target this form of training and get the intensity high enough to build high levels of recruitment. This problem is solved with the Heavy Roller! title: Sloper Scoop, Slopers & Kinetic Chains - CPC minutes
text:
Sloper Scoop - Slopers place higher demands on closed kinetic chains.
When trying to control slopers, one key concept that comes into play is the kinetic chain. 

Our extremities can be viewed as a series of rigid, overlapping segments. Combinations of several successively arranged joints constituting a complex motor unit are called Kinetic Chains. The movements that occur within these segments present as two primary types—
Open Kinetic Chain (OKC) in which the end of the chain (hand or foot) is free to move. 
and
Closed Kinetic Chain (CKC).
Controlling a sloper is CKC - the hand is in contact with a hold and meets resistance that restricts free movement. When one link in the chain - hand, wrist, elbow, shoulders, hips... cannot maintain ideal position, the other joints have to compensate. When this is not possible any more, the chain breaks!
(the weakest link in action!)

There are three ways that a closed kinetic chain is challenged from sloper usage: 
1) Control through tension, 
2) Center of mass adjustment, and 
3) Optimal force production.

We can see this play out in the example here of Kokoro. First, he performs an open-chain move and the pelvis rotates and legs twist as a result. By quickly engaging his core, smearing the right foot for stabilization, and then recognizing a good placement for the left foot, he is able to maintain control through tension and keep his center of mass close to the wall (as opposed to pulling the body away without feet on).

He's then able to generate force from the left leg through the kinetic chain which allows him to accelerate more quickly to the next hold. If there was a lack of core or lower limb engagement, the center of mass would have been far from the wall, the body would not be in an ideal position to keep tension and produce force, and it would have been very difficult to finish this boulder (indeed, Kokoro was the only one who managed).

Don't neglect engaging your full kinetic chain when battling with a sloper!

title: Climbing Technique Tips: How do I stay on slopers?
text:
Slopers are tough for all of us, but they don't have to be!

One of our trainers walks you through what makes slopers hard to hold (spoiler alert: they are round and bulbous shaped holds that you can't pinch or wrap your fingers around. Grabbing one is a lot like palming a basketball) and how you can improve staying on them. 

There are three things to keep in mind when you use slopers. 

1) You want to grab as much surface area as possible. Slopers require friction, so the more surface area you use, the more likely you are to stay on. 

2) Body positioning is incredibly important and the goal here is to position your body so that you're pulling on the hold as little as possible. Position your body below the hold—if you pull straight out, you'll pull yourself right off the hold. 

3) Slopers can still be hard, even with the best technique. It helps to build hand and wrist strength and you can do that by practicing slopers. 

To do so, head over to a training board and adjust it to vertical. Find a sloper that feels friendly to you. Find good footholds and a good hand that allows you to hold the sloper with one arm straight and your weight directly beneath it. Hold this position for 10-15 seconds at a time.

Rest and repeat this exercise for up to 5 times per side. Repeat once a week. If the exercise starts to feel easy, find a harder sloper to train on and/or increase the wall angle.

For more technique tips like this one, check out an upcoming class near you: https://movementgyms.com/introduction...

Slopers have always been my nemesis!! Join me as Louis from @CatalystClimbing coaches me through some of the hardest sloper problems in the gym (and makes them look V2)...

Let us know if we missed any top tips!!!

There's no official sponsor for this video, so here are some codes that give me commission if you want some cool stuff with the added bonus supporting me 🙃

✅ 10% off Rúngne with code ANNA10:
https://rungne.com
✅ 10USD off Tindeq with code HAZELNUTT
https://tindeq.com

Or consider joining my Patreon— Bonus content and blog updates galore!
https://www.patreon.com/annahazelnutt

And if you're confused about the timeline, you're correct in thinking this is not a current video 🙈 I'm only 5 months late on this edit lolol. We filmed this back in May when we did the flexibility video in London. I am currently still dealing with wrist issues in Canada (go figure!! weak wrists!!) but am hoping to be climbing again soon :P 

Find us on socials:
Louis/Catalyst Climbing: https://www.instagram.com/catalystclimbing/
Me: https://www.instagram.com/annahazelnutt/

00:00 intro
01:24 steps 1-3 for coaching slopers
02:15 strong openhand grip
02:19 wrist strength
02:23 compression strength
03:40 be intentional about direction
03:55 blind optimism
04:02 perseverance
04:35 don't crimp...
04:49 friction matters
04:51 brush the holds
04:54 cool hands down
06:22 be patient

07:56 chalky hands
08:49 switch problems?
11:53 celebrate small improvements
13:15 try more than 3 times
13:48 find stronger body positions (whoops, two tip #16's haha)

title: Don't Sweat the Technique #5: Tips for Grips, Crimps and Slopers.
text:
Don't Sweat the Technique #5: Tips for Grips, Crimps and Slopers.
Northside Boulders presents a series of climbing technique tips. This week we look at different grip types, tricks to make holds juggier and tips for injury prevention.

title: Lead finals | Koper 2026
text:
Koper, Slovenia, welcomes the World Climbing Series for a fifth consecutive year on 4 and 5 September 2026. The event is Slovenia’s 30th international Lead competition, following 25 editions held in Kranj.
